title: Password Hashing with Passlib
description: Safely store passwords using bcrypt hashing.

slides.title: Why Hash Passwords? 🔒
slides.content:
# Never Store Plain Text Passwords!

Hashing transforms a password into a fixed-length string that cannot be reversed. When a user logs in, you hash the provided password and compare with the stored hash.

**Use bcrypt** – it's slow and resistant to brute-force attacks.

slides.title: Hashing with Passlib
slides.codeSnippet:
from passlib.context import CryptContext

pwd_context = CryptContext(schemes=["bcrypt"], deprecated="auto")

hashed = pwd_context.hash("mypassword")
print(hashed)  # $2b$12$...
print(pwd_context.verify("mypassword", hashed))  # True

quizData.question: Why is bcrypt preferred over simple hash functions like MD5 for passwords?

options.text: It is intentionally slow, making brute-force harder

quizData.explanation: bcrypt is a key derivation function designed to be slow, which helps mitigate brute-force attacks.
